paras: The attempted lynching of Ed Grayham took place at Brookhaven, Mississippi, on a Saturday at the end of December 1881, when a large number of men came to the town jail to lynch Ed. Grayham, a young Black prisoner accused of raping a girl of about five. The jailer had sent the prisoner away in advance, and the men left after searching the empty jail. Grayham, spelled Graham in later reports, was convicted of rape in February 1882 and sentenced to life in the penitentiary.

According to the Brookhaven Ledger, Grayham was accused of having "outraged" the roughly five-year-old daughter of J. Q. Rawls on November 24, 1881. He was arrested soon afterward, tried before Justice W. C. Price, committed by him, and brought to town by Rawls himself. In the weeks that followed, talk of a lynching circulated widely enough that the jailer, Mr. Mikell, heard a demand for the keys would be made.

On the Saturday before the Ledger's January 5, 1882 issue, probably December 31, 1881, a large body of men from beat three appeared in Brookhaven and said they had come to lynch Grayham. When they demanded the keys to the jail, Mikell told them the prisoner was not there and let them examine the jail to see for themselves. Having been warned, he had already sent Grayham away, and he promised to protect him until the circuit court met on the fourth Monday of January. No violence was reported.

On February 2 the Ledger reported a street rumor that the grand jury had indicted Ed. Graham for rape. Two weeks later it reported that he had been found guilty and sentenced to the penitentiary for life. The Panola Weekly Star repeated that at the recent term of court in Brookhaven "Ed. Graham, rapist," had been sent to the penitentiary for life.

The Brookhaven Ledger ran the fullest account under the headline "Wanted to Lynch Him," calling the prisoner "the brute" and treating the charge as established. Its editor wrote that had the men lynched him "at the time, the deed might have been excusable," but that they had waited too long and "talked too much about it to succeed." The paper did not condemn lynching as such, and it reported without criticism the jailer's pledge to protect the prisoner until court.

The story spread as brief state-news paragraphs: the Jackson Weekly Clarion credited the Ledger on January 11, dropped Grayham's name for "a colored boy," and kept the word "brute." The Memphis Daily Appeal gave it one line among its "Mississippi Morsels" on January 15.

The reprints differ on how the prisoner was protected. The local Ledger says jailer Mikell sent him off before the men arrived, while the Clarion, though citing the Ledger, says "the Sheriff had placed him beyond the reach of the crowd." The Memphis Appeal says instead that he "was got safely into jail"; the Ledger, the only local and first-hand report, is the fuller account.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Grayham
bases: A large body of men came to the Brookhaven jail announcing they would lynch a prisoner and demanded the keys, but he had been removed and no one was harmed (A1, A2, A3).

A 'large number of men' came to lynch Grayham over an accusation of rape, acting without legal authority, but he had been sent away and was later tried and sentenced, so no one was killed (A1, A2, A5).

The attempt is known from the Brookhaven Ledger (A1); the Jackson Clarion's paragraph is credited to the Ledger (A2) and the Memphis Appeal's unattributed one-line item (A3) adds no independent detail, while the indictment and sentence are reported by the Ledger (A4, A5) and the Panola Star (A6).
